We demonstrate that unsupervised preprocessing can, in fact, introduce a substantial bias into cross-validation estimates"
Kapoor & Narayanan 2023: "[L1.2] Pre-processing on training and test set."

findings.row: §4 'Median fill: allowed in-fold' and 'Categories as the analysis model: rank lower, state the information loss' (prediction)
findings.claim_in_spec: Median fill is allowed in-fold under prediction. Categorizing continuous predictors is ranked lower, with the information loss stated.
findings.customary: Both are common practice in prediction work.
findings.sound: Constant imputation in-fold is consistent for prediction when missingness is not informative, and missing-incorporated-in-attribute handles informative missingness for trees. Categorizing continuous predictors loses information.
findings.correction: None. Optionally offer missing indicators / MIA when missingness may be informative (Sperrin 2020).
sources: Josse et al., 'On the consistency of supervised learning with missing values' (arXiv:1902.06931, rev. 2024): "the widely-used method of imputing with a constant, such as the mean prior to learning is consistent when missing values are not informative"; "we recommend using the 'missing incorporated in attribute' method as it can handle both non-informative and informative missing values."

Altman & Royston, BMJ 2006;332:1080: "Dichotomising a variable at the median reduces power by the same amount as would discarding a third of the data."; "a carefully developed model with bilirubin as a continuous explanatory variable explained 31% more of the variability in the data than when bilirubin distribution was split at the median."

summary:
Adversarial review of the prediction column of docs/turbotab-next/MODELING_SEQUENCE.md: §1 rows 1, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 and the §4 prediction leash rows. I checked them against primary sources (PMC, arXiv, Europe PMC full text, BMJ via ORA, CRAN) and against the engine code that implements them. The session's WebSearch budget ran out partway, so later sources were read through WebFetch and the Europe PMC API.

Holds (with its source): in-fold feature construction (row 7); in-fold median fill; ranking categorization lower; ranking a single split below resampling at small n. The last needs three refinements: repeated CV for near-interpolating learners, at least 500 bootstraps per Collins 2024 (the engine default is 200), and the Iba 2021 small-n caveat.

Critical, 1 finding: Explore 'on training rows only' is a leash that is too loose. Below 20,000 units the app's own validation plan has no holdout, so training rows are all rows. Any lever pulled from an outcome-relationship view (a spline from a bending plot, dropping a weak predictor) then sits outside the bootstrap/CV, yet the score is labeled optimism-corrected. Fix: record those views as looked at, offer every Explore lever as an in-fold rule the resampling repeats, and disclose any choice made by hand.

Major, 10 findings:
- **Selection (row 8):** customary options (stepwise, VIP > 1, univariable screens, variance filters) are missing from the menu. Out-of-fold selection should be refused, TRIPOD+AI 9a pre-selection asked, and inclusion frequencies reported.
- **Shelf (row 9):** order it by soundness at this size, not 'expected performance'. Put a Riley sample-size step before it and fit a regression-with-splines benchmark every time.
- **'Price of explainability':** rename it to the cost or gain of the interpretable model (Rudin). Measure it as a signed paired difference on a proper score and calibration, corrected for the choice of the best flexible family.
- **Primary metric (row 11):** the spec says 'proper scores first', but the engine compares, selects and declares binary, ordinal and time-to-event models on AUC/C, which STRATOS calls semi-proper.
- **Comparisons (row 11):** under the default bootstrap validation they rest on one 5-fold partition (rows.py:1734). Repeated k-fold should be the substrate for paired corrected t, the baseline verdict and BBC-CV. The row's 'nested CV' wording should name BBC-CV for the family choice.
- **CV intervals (row 11):** they describe the expected performance of the modeling procedure, not this fitted model (Bates et al.). At p ≫ n they undercover badly (31% vs 10% miscoverage at n = 90, p = 1000); offer the nested-CV interval or label the standard one.
- **Calibration (row 11):** not computed for time-to-event, ordinal or multiclass outcomes.
- **Declaration (row 12):** with no holdout, the result must be the selection-corrected estimate, not the winning family's bootstrap-corrected score alone.
- **TRIPOD+AI gaps:** items 10, 12d/23b, 12e (net benefit), 12f (shrinkage), 13, 14, 15 and 23a are produced by no step.

Minor, 2 findings: stability selection should be labeled as error control (a reproducible predictor panel), not a prediction optimizer, and ranked after elastic net. North star 5's 'calibration-preserving weighting' is a misnomer: every imbalance correction miscalibrates, and threshold shifting is the sound alternative.

Engine paths cited: /Users/nhedglin/tabular-ml-lab/turbotab/core/models/metrics.py (PRIMARY, METRICS), /Users/nhedglin/tabular-ml-lab/turbotab/core/stages/rows.py:1734 (repeats only under repeated_kfold), /Users/nhedglin/tabular-ml-lab/turbotab/core/models/validation.py (validation_plan, _calibration_points), /Users/nhedglin/tabular-ml-lab/turbotab/core/models/selection.py (BBC-CV), /Users/nhedglin/tabular-ml-lab/turbotab/core/decisions.py:280 (OPTIMISM_BOOT = 200). No files in the repo were written.

I reviewed Section 1 rows 5 and 6, the domain relations in §2, and the domain parts of §4 and §13 against primary sources. I also checked turbotab/core to see what each chain actually produces. The energy rulings hold: the residual method keeps total energy, all-components ranks first for substitution under inference, and a model that omits an energy source is blocked and recorded. QC-RLSC before the seal on reference rows also holds, as does omics normalization in-fold.

The spec fails on the order in which steps combine. These findings would change what the app does or says:

1. **Critical: multiple imputation (MI) ignores the terms the analysis model uses.** MI runs on raw columns with a linear-normal model. The log residual, density, spline, interaction and omics log2 are then derived from the imputed values in each completed table (passive imputation). In Bartlett 2015 this pulls a quadratic coefficient to 0.70 instead of 1.0, and its 95% interval never covers the truth (coverage 0%). Normal draws can also be negative for skewed intakes and intensities. A log of a negative or zero value then either errors or becomes missing, and the in-pipeline median fill fills it. That puts a single median fill inside the pooled inference table, which §4 blocks.
2. **Major: regression calibration (RC) conflicts with the top-ranked energy model.** Freedman 2011 limits univariate RC to energy-adjusted intakes (residual or density). The code refuses RC under all-components, standard and partition, but the spec offers both RC and all-components first without naming that trade-off.
3. **Major: RC is not labeled or placed correctly.** RC from repeated recalls corrects only day-to-day error, and it belongs beside the uncorrected estimate rather than replacing it. Under MI it currently refits one outcome-free fill instead of running inside each imputed table.
4. **Major: the log/substitution label is wrong.** The spec says a log makes the substitution a "ratio rather than difference". In fact the curve is still a kcal swap, but its effect now varies with each person's intake, and the all-components weighted contrast is undefined on logged components. The menu also lacks compositional (ilr) models under inference.
5. **Major: "residual equals standard model" is false once a spline or categories are applied** to the adjusted nutrient, yet the label stays the same.
6. **Major: batch handling is missing from the sequence.** This includes the Nygaard 2016 ComBat pitfall: removing batch effects while protecting the outcome inflates group differences.
7. **Major: non-detects are handled out of order.** The omics chain logs before handling missing values, so non-detects turn into median fills.
8. **Major: survey scales use the wrong reliability and order.** Alpha should be omega. Attenuation must use reliability conditional on the covariates. Missing items need item-level MI before scoring.
9. **Minor:** some data-scope labels are wrong (PQN can be reference-rows scope, the D-ratio filter needs the training fold, scoring by a published key is row-local). Also, m should be at least the percentage of incomplete rows, and the leave-one-out model is missing from the menu.

One gap: I could not retrieve a primary source stating that the nutrient and energy are logged before the residual. That claim rests on NUTRITION_PACK §04 as the field default. My web-search budget ran out partway through, so I took the remaining abstracts from PubMed via NCBI E-utilities.

findings.row: §1 row 6 (Missing data, inference) x row 4 (functional form) x row 5 (energy/omics transforms) x row 7 (declared interactions); §2 'multiple imputation invalidates median fill ... implies pooled intervals'
findings.claim_in_spec: Inference: 'multiple imputation with the outcome and energy, m >= 20, Rubin's rules'. Nothing requires the imputation model to be compatible with the analysis model's nonlinear or derived terms. Implemented chain (/Users/nhedglin/tabular-ml-lab/turbotab/core/models/pipeline.py docstring 'Step order: detect -> normalize -> impute -> energy adjustment -> exposure form'; methods/missing.py imputation_frame): MI imputes the raw inputs plus the outcome with Bayesian linear-normal draws, deliberately untransformed (methods/imputation.py lines 20-30). Each completed table then derives the log residual, density N/E, spline basis, interaction and omics PQN+log2 passively.
findings.correction: Add a §2 relation: 'a declared nonlinear or derived term (spline, log, ratio/density, log-log residual, interaction, omics log) under MI -> the imputation model must be compatible with the analysis model.' The order follows from the term. (1) Linear residual, with or without energy kept: impute N, E and Y, then compute the residual in each completed table, re-estimating b each time. This is compatible because the model stays linear in N and E, so keep this order. (2) Log or log-log residual, and log-analysed intakes or intensities: impute on the log scale (transform, then impute), so draws stay positive and the imputation and analysis share a scale. (3) Spline, interaction or density with a linear outcome model: use SMC-FCS, or 'just another variable' (JAV) as second best. With a logistic or Cox outcome, use SMC-FCS only; JAV should not be used for logistic regression. (4) Identities among energy sources: impute the sources and 'other', then derive E as their sum, so 'other' = E - Σ sources is never negative. Leash under inference: block and record 'passive MI with a declared nonlinear term', and state that the nonlinearity and interaction tests are biased toward the null. A NaN produced after a log inside a completed table must never reach the in-pipeline median imputer. It must be refused or routed to the detection-limit (LOD) question, because today it puts a single median fill into the pooled inference table that §4 blocks.
findings.customary: Impute-then-transform (passive imputation) is the default in mice and ice and is what most papers do (Bartlett 2015 describes it as the default).
findings.sound: Substantive-model-compatible FCS (SMC-FCS) is consistent for squared, interaction and nonlinear (Cox, logistic) models under MAR. Passive imputation attenuates the nonlinear term with near-zero interval coverage.
sources: Bartlett, Seaman, White & Carpenter 2015, Stat Methods Med Res 24:462-487: "X2 is then passively imputed by squaring the imputed X values. In this case, estimates of the parameters of the substantive model from multiply imputed datasets will be biased (unless the quadratic coefficient is in truth zero)"; Table 2, normal X MCAR, linear passive: "0.696 (0.041) 0.0" (true value 1, coverage 0%), versus SMC-FCS "0.998 (0.038) 93.9".

Seaman, Bartlett & White 2012, BMC Med Res Methodol 12:46: "JAV is the best of a set of imperfect imputation methods for linear regression with a quadratic or interaction effect, but should not be used for logistic regression."

White, Pandis & Pham, 'Missing data 6. Choices in doing multiple imputation' (UCL Discovery 10158712): "A particular issue arises if the analysis model explores interactions or non-linear effects, because then the imputation model needs to be complex enough to respect these complexities"; "imputing and analysing on different scales can be problematic".

van Buuren, Flexible Imputation of Missing Data 2nd ed., §6.3.2: "Include all variables that appear in the complete-data model, i.e., the model that will be applied to the data after imputation, including the outcome".

findings.row: §1 row 5 inference ('energy model ... all-components first for substitution' AND 'regression calibration when there are repeated recalls'); §2 has no relation between them
findings.claim_in_spec: Row 5 offers all-components first for substitution and regression calibration (RC) for repeated recalls as independent items, with no relation between them. The code refuses RC under all-components, standard and partition (turbotab/core/stages/calibration.py lines 20-24, 'The multivariate method is not offered').
findings.correction: Add a §2 conflict: 'regression calibration conflicts with all-components, standard and partition until multivariate RC exists.' Name the trade-off in one line on the energy-model question when repeated recalls exist. All-components has no composite-variable bias, but its error-prone components stay uncorrected and the errors of several mismeasured terms can bias in either direction. Residual or density can be calibrated (univariate RC), but they carry composite-variable bias. Add an 'implies' relation: RC implies that every outcome-model covariate enters the calibration equation (and never the outcome). Add an order rule: energy-adjust each recall day first, then calibrate the energy-adjusted exposure. Multivariate RC (Rosner 1990) is the route that would let all-components be calibrated; list it on the menu as not yet available rather than leaving it absent.
findings.customary: Univariate RC of energy-adjusted intakes (densities or residuals), and multivariate RC (Rosner 1990) for the standard and partition models, are both customary in cohort studies (Freedman 2011).
findings.sound: Univariate RC of a raw nutrient beside error-prone energy or other components is unsound: the attenuation factor is wrong and the bias can go either way.
sources: Freedman, Schatzkin, Midthune & Kipnis 2011, J Natl Cancer Inst 103:1086 (abstract): "performing statistical adjustment of relative risks ... using univariate (only for energy-adjusted intakes such as densities or residuals) or multivariate regression calibration."

Rosner, Spiegelman & Willett 1990, Am J Epidemiol 132:734 (abstract): "if several risk factors for disease are considered in the same multiple logistic regression model, and some of these risk factors are measured with error, the point and interval estimates of relative risk corresponding to any of these factors may be biased either toward or away from the null value."
Kipnis et al. 2009, Biometrics 65:1003 (abstract): "individual usual intake is generally predicted as the conditional mean intake given 24HR-reported intake and other covariates in the health model."

Keogh, Shaw & Gustafson 2020 (STRATOS Part 1), Stat Med 39:2197, §6.1.1: the worked example calibrates the energy-adjusted exposure ("the prediction equation for log potassium density intake is: −0.48+0.45×log(FFQ potassium density)+0.046×sex+0.0059×age"), with the outcome-model covariates in the calibration equation.

findings.row: §1 row 5 inference 'regression calibration when there are repeated recalls'; its order relative to row 6 (MI) and its place relative to row 11 (declared secondary analyses)
findings.claim_in_spec: RC appears as a domain transform of the reported model, with no stated assumption, no placement as a secondary analysis, and no order relative to MI. Under MI the code calibrates one outcome-free single fill (turbotab/core/stages/calibration.py line 396: 'The calibration refits the model with blanks filled once without the outcome').
findings.correction: (1) Label: replicate 24-hour recalls correct only within-person (day-to-day) error, under the assumption that recalls are unbiased for usual intake. Person-specific reporting bias remains, so the corrected estimate is still attenuated and can be off in either direction. Label it customary, with soundness conditional on that assumption. (2) Placement: report the corrected estimate as a declared secondary analysis beside the uncorrected one (row 11). The test of no association stays the uncorrected model's. Intervals come from bootstrapping the whole procedure. (3) Order under inference: run MI first, with the recall mean or recalls, Z and the outcome in the imputation model. Then fit RC inside each completed table, with the calibration equation containing Z but never Y. Combine bootstrap and MI with a scheme shown to be valid (Schomaker & Heumann 2018), not a single fill. (4) Generalize the §2 relation 'MI implies pooled intervals (Rubin's rules) everywhere a coefficient is shown': outputs whose intervals come from a bootstrap (RC intervals, substitution-curve bands) need a stated bootstrap-with-MI scheme.
findings.customary: Treating replicate 24-hour recalls as unbiased is widespread practice (Beaton et al.; NCI method).
findings.sound: Self-report error is not classical, so recall-based RC under-corrects. Biomarker calibration is the only unbiased reference, available for energy, protein, potassium and sodium.
sources: Keogh, Shaw & Gustafson 2020 (STRATOS Part 1), Stat Med 39:2197, §4.3.1: "The measurement error model for self-reported dietary intakes has been shown not to conform to the classical model, so replicates studies are not a true option. However, many investigators, in the absence of anything better, have adopted the assumption that 24-hour recalls provide unbiased measurements"; §6.1.2: "one cannot use the usual model standard errors from the outcome regression model when performing RC, as these will be too small".
Kipnis et al. 2003, Am J Epidemiol 158:14 (OPEN, abstract): "Using the 24HR as a reference instrument can seriously underestimate true attenuation (up to 60% for energy-adjusted protein)."

Freedman et al. 2011, J Natl Cancer Inst 103:1086 (abstract): "reporting estimates adjusted for measurement error along with the usual relative risk estimates"; "statistical significance tests of unadjusted relative risk estimates are approximately valid."
Schomaker & Heumann 2018, Stat Med 37:2252 (abstract): "We present 4 methods that ... combine bootstrap estimation with multiple imputation. We show that 3 of the 4 approaches yield valid inference".

findings.row: §2 'log transform of a nutrient changes what a substitution means (ratio rather than difference) — the curve's label says so'; order of log vs residual; ilr offered under prediction only (row 5)
findings.claim_in_spec: A log turns the substitution into a ratio instead of a difference, and the curve's label says so.
findings.correction: The label is wrong for the instrument the app actually computes. The substitution curve (turbotab/core/methods/substitution.py) moves k kcal from donor to recipient through the fitted pipeline, so it stays an isocaloric kcal difference. Replace the relation with three statements. (a) Under any log (log-log residual, log N in the outcome model, logged components), the effect of moving k kcal is no longer a constant per-kcal coefficient contrast. It depends on each person's baseline intake and on k, and the curve is an average of heterogeneous row-level effects; label it that way. (b) The all-components relative effect (a source's coefficient minus a share-weighted average of the others) is undefined on logged components, because Tomova's substitution models require every variable in the same units (kcal). Under inference, refuse reading a substitution off logged coefficients and allow only the standardized (g-computation) curve. (c) Order: a log comes before the residual (log N ~ log E, then back-transform), never residual-then-log (residual plus constant can be ≤ 0, and the log of a linear residual has no estimand) and never mixed scales (log N on raw E). Under inference, add compositional isometric log-ratio (ilr) models to the menu as the principled log-scale model of dietary composition, labeled emerging. At present ilr is offered only under prediction, which shortens the inference menu.
findings.customary: Willett log-log residual (NUTRITION_PACK §04 methods sentence; I could not retrieve a primary-source quote for log-before-residual). Linear-in-kcal substitution models (Tomova 2022a/b).
findings.sound: Substitution contrasts are coefficient differences only on a common linear kcal scale. On a log scale, only a standardized contrast at stated intakes, or an ilr model, has a defined estimand.
sources: Tomova, Gilthorpe & Tennant 2022, Am J Clin Nutr (doi 10.1093/ajcn/nqac188), abstract: the leave-one-out and energy partition models performed well "provided all variables were measured in the same units"; "The practice of examining foods measured in grams or portions while adjusting for total energy intake is likely to deliver obscure relative effect estimands with unclear interpretations."

Tomova et al. 2022, Am J Clin Nutr 115:189-198: the average relative causal effect is obtained "by subtracting a weighted average of the estimated effects of all other individual component sources of energy from the total causal effect". This contrast is defined only on a common additive scale.
Leite 2016, Stat Methods Med Res 25:3057 (abstract): "The new isometric log-ratio variables allow full inferences about each element of dietary composition and adjustment by total energy intake."

findings.row: §2 missing relation: row 4 (spline or categories) x row 5 (residual energy model)
findings.claim_in_spec: The residual model is presented as the standard model's estimand. The code labels residual-with-energy 'the standard model's, identically' (turbotab/core/methods/energy.py METHOD_TABLE['residual']) whatever the exposure form. It runs the spline or quintiles after the energy step (pipeline.py: 'the curve or the fifths are of the energy-adjusted intake'), and energy.py has no spline awareness.
findings.correction: Add a relation: 'spline or categories x residual: the identity with the standard model holds only for a linear term.' {N_adj, E} spans the same columns as {N, E}, but a spline basis of N_adj = N - b(E - Ē) with E does not span the same space as a spline of N with E. The curve is therefore a different model with a different estimand: the nutrient's curve on the energy-adjusted scale at mean energy, not the substitution curve at fixed total energy. Change the label when a spline or categories are declared on a residual, and offer standard-model spline(N) + E as the substitution-curve route. Customary residual quintiles stay on the menu with their own estimand sentence.
findings.customary: Quintiles or splines of energy-adjusted residuals are customary.
findings.sound: The equivalence to the standard model is algebraic for a linear term only. Under any nonlinear transform the two are different models.
sources: Tomova et al. 2022, Am J Clin Nutr 115:189-198, on the residual model: "The approach is mathematically identical to the standard model, and therefore also targets the average relative causal effect." That identity is a linear reparametrization and does not survive a nonlinear basis.

McCullough & Byrd 2023, Am J Epidemiol 192:1801: "A variation on the simple nutrient residual model proposed by Willett and Stampfer includes the nutrient residual plus a term for total energy intake."

findings.row: §1 row 5 (omics, both purposes) and §13 'batch handling': batch correction is absent from the sequence and from §2
findings.claim_in_spec: Row 5 lists only 'omics normalization in-fold'. Batch appears only as a future item in §13. No relation covers ComBat, batch as a covariate, or an outcome in the batch model.
findings.correction: Add a batch step to row 5 with purpose-split leashes. Inference: account for batch in the outcome model (fixed effect or random intercept), ranked first. ComBat-style adjustment with the outcome as a protected covariate is blocked and recorded whenever outcome groups are unbalanced across batches, because it inflates group differences. ComBat without the outcome is stated to deflate them under imbalance. Prediction: batch adjustment is fitted in-fold and never with the outcome in its model (refuse: label leakage). Use the training set as the reference batch (reference ComBat) or addon adjustment, so held-out and new rows are adjusted without changing the training values. Metabolomics with pooled QCs: inter-batch alignment by QC-RLSC is reference-rows scope before the seal (§13), and that relation should say it covers batches as well as drift. Scopes: QC-based = reference rows; ComBat = training fold; batch covariate = the model.
findings.customary: Running ComBat (Johnson et al. 2007) with the group or outcome in its model matrix, on the full data, before analysis, is widespread.
findings.sound: With unbalanced designs, model batch in the analysis (Nygaard 2016). For prediction, use a fixed reference (training) batch so the training data and model are frozen (Zhang 2018; Hornung 2017).
sources: Nygaard, Rødland & Hovig 2016, Biostatistics 17:29-39 (abstract): "when study groups are not evenly distributed across batches ... batch adjustments may bias, usually deflate, group differences ... using a two-way ANOVA model to simultaneously estimate both group and batch effects ... may systematically induce incorrect group differences in downstream analyses"; body: "For an investigator facing an unbalanced data set with batch effects, our primary advice would be to account for batch in the statistical analysis."

Zhang, Jenkins, Manimaran & Johnson 2018, BMC Bioinformatics 19:262: "establishing the training set as a 'reference batch' to which all future batches will be standardized ... would allow the training data and biomarker to be fixed a priori"; ComBat "suffers from sample 'set bias'".

Hornung, Causeur, Bernau & Boulesteix 2017, Bioinformatics 33:397 (abstract): "We suggest the use of addon normalization and addon batch effect removal techniques in this context to reduce systematic differences between external data and the original dataset".

Dunn et al. 2011, Nat Protoc 6:1060 (abstract): "Methods for quality control-based robust LOESS signal correction to provide signal correction and integration of data from multiple analytical batches are also described."

findings.row: §13 omics chain (drift -> QC rows leave -> seal -> PQN, log, scaling in-fold) and §1 rows 5-6: non-detects/LOD and missing-value order
findings.claim_in_spec: The chain has no missing-value or LOD step. Rows 5 and 6 never mention values below detection. Code: QuotientLog makes zeros missing after log2 ('A zero cannot be logged: it becomes missing', turbotab/core/methods/omics.py line 37). The in-pipeline median or energy-aware imputer, present even under MI (pipeline.py: impute = strategy in ('impute', 'multiple_imputation')), then fills those post-log missing values. Non-detects end up in the middle of the distribution, including inside the pooled inference table.
findings.correction: Make the chain: QC drift and inter-batch correction (reference rows) -> QC-RSD and QC detection-rate filters (reference rows) -> QC rows leave -> seal -> PQN (in-fold, or a QC reference: see the scope finding) -> censoring-aware handling of non-detects and zeros -> log/glog -> scaling (in-fold). Leash: half-minimum or half-LOD fill is allowed with its customary label only when ≤10% of values are censored. Above that, it ranks lower under prediction (QRILC or censored-normal expectation instead) and is blocked and recorded under inference (censored-normal MI within the chained equations instead). A zero that a log would turn into missing must route to the LOD question, never to median fill. Under inference with p ≫ n features, chained-equations MI over every feature is infeasible (the code refuses more than 80 columns). State the route: per-feature censoring-aware imputation with a restricted predictor set (about 15 predictors), or complete-feature analysis with its assumption stated.
findings.customary: MetaboAnalyst half-minimum fill; workflow order normalisation -> imputation -> transformation -> scaling (Di Guida 2016).
findings.sound: Non-detects are left-censored (MNAR), not MAR. Half-LOD is biased beyond about 5-10% censoring. Tobit/censored MI or QRILC is sound.
sources: Di Guida et al. 2016, Metabolomics 12:93 (abstract): "The generic metabolomics data processing workflow is constructed with a serial set of processes including peak picking, quality assurance, normalisation, missing value imputation, transformation and scaling."

Lubin et al. 2004, Environ Health Perspect 112:1691 (abstract): "assignment of one-half the detection limit to nondetected values ... can be biased unless the percentage of measurements below detection limits is small (5-10%) ... Truncated data methods (e.g., Tobit regression) and multiple imputation offer two unbiased approaches".
Wei et al. 2018, Sci Rep 8:663 (abstract): "RF performed the best for MCAR/MAR and QRILC was the favored one for left-censored MNAR."
van Buuren, FIMD 2nd ed. §6.3.2: "the increase in explained variance in linear regression is typically negligible after the best, say, 15 variables have been included."

findings.row: §1 row 5 inference 'scale scores with reliability and attenuation'; prediction 'scale scores'; order relative to row 6
findings.claim_in_spec: Scale scores come with 'reliability and attenuation'. The spec does not name the reliability coefficient, does not say whether attenuation is conditional on covariates, and gives no order with MI or data scope.
findings.correction: (1) Reliability: compute omega and say which one (omega-total for a unidimensional congeneric scale, omega-hierarchical for a multidimensional one). Show alpha only with its customary label, because alpha's assumptions usually fail and it usually understates reliability. Disattenuating by alpha over-corrects. (2) Attenuation: in a model with covariates Z, the slope is attenuated by the reliability conditional on Z, not by the scale's marginal omega. Dividing by marginal omega under-corrects whenever the scale correlates with the covariates. Offer a latent-variable (SEM) model or a conditional-reliability correction, and report the disattenuated estimate as a declared secondary analysis beside the observed one. (3) Order under inference: when items are missing, run item-level MI before scoring, not MI of the total score. Prorate by the instrument's manual (row-local) only when few items are missing. Mean imputation is blocked and recorded. (4) Prediction: no disattenuation, because the deployed model sees the same error-prone score. (5) Scopes: scoring by a published key, reverse coding and prorating are row-local. IRT or factor scores and sample z-scores are training fold. Reliability is descriptive under prediction.
findings.customary: Cronbach's alpha reporting; Spearman correction by alpha; prorated sum scores.
findings.sound: Omega family reliability (McNeish 2018); covariate-conditional attenuation factor (STRATOS); item-level MI (Eekhout 2014).
sources: McNeish 2018, Psychol Methods 23:412 (abstract): "Cronbach's alpha is riddled with problems stemming from unrealistic assumptions. In many circumstances, violating these assumptions yields estimates of reliability that are too small"; alternatives named: "omega total, Revelle's omega total, the greatest lower bound, and Coefficient H".

Keogh, Shaw & Gustafson 2020 (STRATOS Part 1), Stat Med 39:2197, §3.1.2: with covariates Z, "the relationship β*X = λβX still holds but now λ = αX|Z var(X|Z) / (α²X|Z var(X|Z) + var(U))"; §1: "In studies in which the aim is instead to derive a prediction model, the considerations surrounding error-prone variables can be quite different."

Eekhout et al. 2014, J Clin Epidemiol 67:335 (abstract): "Mean imputation caused biased estimates in every missing data scenario when data are missing for more than 10% of the subjects. Furthermore, when a large percentage of subjects had missing items (>25%), MI methods applied to the items outperformed methods applied to the total score."

findings.row: Data scopes in §13 and row 5: PQN, QC filters, log, LOD fill, count normalization
findings.claim_in_spec: §13: 'PQN learns its reference spectrum from study samples, so its scope is training fold.' Row 5 says 'omics normalization in-fold' for everything. No scope is stated for QC feature filters, the log, LOD fills or scale scoring.
findings.correction: State a scope per variant. PQN with a pooled-QC reference spectrum is reference-rows scope and may run before the seal. This is the default in pmp, a common MS pipeline. PQN with a study-sample median reference is training-fold scope, as in the current code. QC-RSD (<20% LC-MS / <30% GC-MS) and QC detection-rate filters are reference rows. The D-ratio filter is the ratio of QC to study-sample dispersion, so it reads participants and is training-fold scope; it cannot run before the seal. A log or glog with a fixed offset is row-local. A half-minimum LOD fill is training fold, while a known instrument LOD is row-local. edgeR log-CPM (prior scaled by the mean library size) and TMM are training fold, as implemented. Each scope is what the lockbox §06 test should decide, so the menu should show it.
findings.customary: Both PQN reference choices are used (Dieterle 2006; pmp defaults to QC). QC RSD and D-ratio filtering (Broadhurst 2018).
findings.sound: Scope follows the §06 test: does row i's output depend on other participants' rows or on the outcome?
sources: pmp (Bioconductor) pqn_normalisation documentation: "For every feature the mean response is calculated across all QC samples. A reference vector is then generated"; when ref_mean is NULL, "QC sample data will be used".

Dieterle et al. 2006, Anal Chem 78:4281 (abstract): PQN is "based on the calculation of a most probable dilution factor by looking at the distribution of the quotients of the amplitudes of a test spectrum by those of a reference spectrum."

Broadhurst et al. 2018, Metabolomics 14:72: "acceptance criterion for RSD is typically set to < 20% ... or < 30%"; "the acceptance criterion for D-ratio is set to, at most, < 50%"; "The acceptance criterion for detection rate is typically set to > 70%".

findings.row: §1 row 6 inference 'm ≥ 20'
findings.correction: State m ≥ max(20, the percentage of rows with any imputed value), and report Monte Carlo error. The code already warns about this (methods/missing.py mi_concerns); the spec and the methods sentence should say it so the default scales with missingness.
findings.customary: m = 5-20 is common in practice.
findings.sound: m ≥ the percentage of incomplete cases, so pooled p-values and intervals reproduce (White, Royston & Wood 2011).
sources: White, Pandis & Pham, 'Missing data 6. Choices in doing multiple imputation' (UCL Discovery 10158712), citing White, Royston & Wood 2011, Stat Med 30:377: "A rule of thumb is that the number of imputations should be at least equal to the percentage of incomplete cases ... More important is to use one's statistical software to report the Monte Carlo errors".

findings.row: §1 row 5 / §2 energy model menu: the leave-one-out substitution model
findings.claim_in_spec: The menu (energy.py METHODS) offers none, standard, residual (two forms), density (two forms), partition and all-components. The leave-one-out model is not named.
findings.correction: Name the leave-one-out model on the menu: total energy plus every source except the one being replaced. It is the most customary substitution model in nutritional cohorts and performs as well as partition for single-component swaps measured in kcal. Rank it beside all-components under inference, with the same omitted-source rule. Sources in grams or portions get the 'obscure estimand' concern.
findings.customary: Leave-one-out is the field's usual substitution model.
findings.sound: Unbiased for a single-component swap when all variables are in the same units; biased when the swap involves more than one substituting component.
sources: Tomova et al. 2022, Am J Clin Nutr 115:189-198: "Robust causal effect estimates could also be obtained using a variant of the standard model ... that in addition adjusted for all but 1 remaining dietary component, an approach that is sometimes termed the 'leave-one-out' approach."

Tomova, Gilthorpe & Tennant 2022, Am J Clin Nutr (nqac188), abstract: the leave-one-out and energy partition models "performed equally well when the target estimand involved substituting a single exposure with a single component, provided all variables were measured in the same units"; "Bias occurred when the substitution involved >1 substituting component".

findings.row: §1 row 5 energy models (residual keeps E; all-components first for substitution under inference; 'choice matters little' under prediction); §2 'energy model constrains substitution ... block and record under inference'
findings.claim_in_spec: The residual method keeps total energy. All-components ranks first for substitution under inference, with its precision cost. Under prediction the choice matters little. Omitted energy sources are blocked and recorded under inference above a stated share.
findings.correction: None, with one wording limit: 'matters little' applies only among models that keep total energy, which are linear reparametrizations of one another. Density-alone and energy-dropped residual discard information. The code's TENSION sentence already says this.
findings.customary: Standard and residual are the field defaults; all-components is emerging and disputed (Willett, Stampfer & Tobias 2022).
findings.sound: All-components avoids composite-variable bias at a precision cost. The residual with E kept equals the standard model.
sources: Tomova et al. 2022, Am J Clin Nutr 115:189-198: "A single model that includes all individual components of the diet may provide the simplest and most accurate approach"; "This strategy does introduce a trade-off between minimizing bias ... and maximizing precision".

McCullough & Byrd 2023, Am J Epidemiol 192:1801: "A variation on the simple nutrient residual model proposed by Willett and Stampfer includes the nutrient residual plus a term for total energy intake."
Tomova, Gilthorpe & Tennant 2022 (nqac188): "Bias occurred when the substitution involved >1 substituting component". This supports blocking and recording omitted sources.

findings.row: §2 'QC drift correction (before the seal; reference-rows scope) implies that the QC rows leave the cohort, and precedes in-fold normalization'; row 5 'omics normalization in-fold'
findings.claim_in_spec: QC-RLSC is learned only from pooled QCs over run order, before the seal. The QC rows then leave the cohort, and normalization is fit in-fold.
findings.correction: None to the order. Add to the drift relation that QC-RLSC is fit per batch, needs a QC at least every 10th injection or at least 5 QCs per batch (otherwise refuse with that reason), and also aligns batches (see the batch finding). In-fold TMM/PQN with a frozen reference applied to held-out rows is sound.
findings.customary: QC-RLSC (Dunn 2011) is the standard for large LC/GC-MS studies.
findings.sound: It learns only from technical replicates, so a participant's corrected value depends on no other participant and not on the outcome.
sources: Dunn et al. 2011, Nat Protoc 6:1060 (abstract): "Methods for quality control-based robust LOESS signal correction to provide signal correction and integration of data from multiple analytical batches are also described."

Broadhurst et al. 2018, Metabolomics 14:72: "it is recommended that a pooled QC is analysed at least every 10th sample, and/or there are at least five pooled QCs distributed evenly across a single batch".

Zhang et al. 2018, BMC Bioinformatics 19:262: whole-set batch adjustment "suffers from sample 'set bias' meaning that if samples or batches are added to or removed from the set ... the adjusted values will be different". This supports fitting references on training rows and freezing them.

summary:
I reviewed §2 and the chain as a whole by building seven analyses end to end against the spec and the engine it governs, read-only. Eleven relations or orderings give a wrong, unreportable or under-covered result in a realistic chain, and only five relations hold as written.

Chain 1. NHANES with linked mortality, log-residual fiber, a spline exposure, Cox, multiple imputation, population estimand. It breaks in four places:
- Step 4 asks for the knots before step 5 changes the exposure (finding 4).
- The multiple-imputation model omits strata, PSUs and weights (finding 2).
- Normal draws on the raw scale give negative intakes, and the log residual then refuses the completed copy. The imputation model is also linear in an exposure the outcome model treats as a spline (finding 3).
- The Cox fit runs unweighted with SRS intervals and only a concern after the user chose 'the surveyed population' (finding 1, critical).
What holds: the event indicator and Nelson–Aalen in the imputation model, and Rubin's ν_com set to the design degrees of freedom (in the code, not stated in the spec).
Required sentence: "Fiber and energy were log-transformed and fiber energy-adjusted by the residual method with total energy retained; adjusted intake entered as a restricted cubic spline (4 knots at the 5th/35th/65th/95th percentiles of observed values, fixed across imputations); covariates were multiply imputed (m=20, substantive-model-compatible FCS including the event indicator, Nelson–Aalen cumulative hazard, energy, and survey strata, PSUs and weights); hazard ratios from survey-weighted Cox regression (Taylor linearization) pooled by Rubin's rules on design degrees of freedom."

Chain 2. Repeated 24-h recalls, regression calibration, all-components substitution. It breaks in three places:
- Calibration (step 5) precedes imputation (step 6), so it cannot include imputed confounders. It is also univariate, and nothing propagates its uncertainty (finding 5).
- The 'log means ratio' relation is wrong (finding 6).
- Under multiple imputation the headline substitution curve uses a single outcome-free fill and ignores the survey design (findings 7 and 1).
Required sentence: "Usual intakes of all energy sources were calibrated jointly with every outcome-model covariate in the calibration model; the substitution is the difference of calibrated coefficients in the all-components model; CIs by a bootstrap resampling PSUs within strata that repeats calibration, imputation and the outcome model."

Chain 3. Metabolomics: QC drift, PQN, log, elastic net under nested CV (prediction). The QC-drift relation and nested CV hold. The spec does not put imputation of values below the detection limit between normalization and log, and treats those blanks as MAR (finding 12). It has no batch relation (finding 10), and no grouped folds for repeat samples (finding 9).
Required sentence: "Drift was corrected per batch by QC-RLSC fitted to pooled QCs only, which were then removed; within each training fold, PQN, detection-limit-aware imputation, log transformation and autoscaling were fitted and applied to the held-out fold; elastic-net parameters were tuned in an inner CV nested in an outer CV."

Chain 4. FFQ diet score, omega, attenuation correction, ordinal outcome. Disattenuating a formative, multidimensional index by its internal consistency produces an inflated coefficient. Even for reflective scales, alpha and omega leave out transient error, and the correction is conditional on covariates and approximate on the proportional-odds scale (finding 13). Under a survey design the ordinal family also falls back to unweighted (finding 1).
Required sentence: "Reliability was estimated as the test–retest ICC from a repeat administration (or a calibration substudy); the corrected coefficient was obtained by regression calibration including all model covariates, with bootstrap CIs re-estimating the reliability; uncorrected and corrected estimates are both reported."

Chain 5. Genomics with p ≫ n, batch, screening and penalized logistic regression. In-fold screening and nested CV hold. Batch correction that keeps the outcome-group differences (ComBat with the outcome as a covariate) is unrouted and produces false differences or leakage (finding 10). The inference twin (many exposures) has no multiplicity relation, although the engine already ships a feature-wise family with Benjamini–Hochberg (finding 11).
Required sentence: "Batch was included as a covariate; ComBat was used for visualization only."

Chain 6. Multi-site cohort, repeated visits, GEE, multiple imputation. The imputation is single-level on long rows with no cluster identifier, so a participant's time-invariant covariate gets different imputed values on different visits, and the ICC and coefficients are biased (finding 8). The repeated-units relation is inference-only and participant-only: it says nothing about sites, small-cluster corrections, grouped folds, or performance heterogeneity across sites (finding 9).
Required sentence: "Missing data were imputed with a two-level model (visits within participants, participants within sites), time-invariant covariates once per participant; GEE with exchangeable working correlation and bias-corrected sandwich SEs (few sites)."

Chain 7. An episodically consumed food (zeros), log, quintiles. A consumers-only analysis is a change of estimand that STROBE-nut nut-14 requires the paper to report, and the spec does not route it (finding 14).

STROBE / TRIPOD+AI items the spec currently lets fail:
- STROBE 12(d) and nut-12.2 (sampling design and weighting): findings 1 and 2.
- nut-12.3 (measurement-error adjustment): findings 5 and 13.
- nut-14 (total population or consumers only): finding 14.
- TRIPOD+AI 12d and 23b (heterogeneity across clusters): finding 9.
- TRIPOD+AI 7 (pre-processing, here batch handling): finding 10.
- TRIPOD+AI 11 (missing data) holds.

Also minor: selection run as a sensitivity analysis under multiple imputation must select by Rubin's rules (finding 15). Choices the user makes from training-row evidence are not repeated inside the folds, so they make the CV comparison optimistic (finding 16).

Caveats:
- My web-search budget ran out partway through. Later sources were read as abstracts through the Europe PMC API.
- These quotes come from the repo's own docstrings or packs and were not re-fetched: the NHANES guideline, White & Royston, Lubin, Freedman, the NUTRITION_PACK spline line, and the METABOLOMICS_PACK multiple-testing line.
- I quoted the Benjamini–Hochberg sentence from memory.
